entries.title: Space Agencies Are Trying to Keep Astronauts From Losing Their Sight
entries.summary: A device currently being used to help octogenarians do self-administered eye exams could be part of future space missions to monitor astronauts’ ocular health.
entries.content:
The European Space Agency is trying to understand why astronauts lose their eyesight in space, in the hope they can figure out how to treat—or even prevent—the condition as looming longer spaceflights heighten the risk of permanent vision damage.

The agency has commissioned British eye-scanning startup Siloton to develop a solution ahead of the international Artemis flights to the moon and other deep space missions. The health tech uses quantum technology to shrink core components used in eye-testing equipment found at optometrists to fit on a photonic chip smaller than a coin.

Founded by physicists in 2020, Siloton is currently working with the UK’s National Health Service to enable patients with retinal conditions to self-scan at home. “The ESA pretty much has the same requirements,” says cofounder and chief technology officer Euan Allen. “It's just in a totally different environment.”

Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) is a collection of eye and brain changes caused by spending prolonged periods in a low-gravity environment, and it impacts around 70 percent of astronauts on the International Space Station, according to NASA. One of the starkest cases is that of NASA astronaut John Phillips, who launched to the ISS in 2005 with 20/20 vision, and splashed down six months later with his vision at 20/100—what’s considered a moderate visual impairment. While he was in space, bodily fluid, uninhibited by gravity, built up in his head, squashing his eyeballs, swelling his optic nerve, and pushing his retina forward.

While returning to Earth can reverse some of the damage, space agencies are concerned by both the operational risk of astronauts losing their vision mid-mission, as well as the longer-term health impacts. “The eye condition SANS is a serious health risk facing astronauts on long missions,” says Rebecca Evernden, director of the UK Space Agency. Medical engineers want to develop their understanding of the condition and the factors causing it so that they can manage any ocular damage, and eventually treat it or even stop it from becoming a problem.

Scientists are already monitoring how spaceflight impacts the human eye on the ISS using a modified version of the device found in optometry offices that measures the thickness of layers at the back of the eye. However, the device is bulky and requires real-time remote guidance from experts on the ground. As astronauts journey further into deep space, lengthening communication delays with Earth will mean this is no longer feasible.

Siloton’s device would allow astronauts to scan their retinas more frequently by automating some of the process so that examinations do not need ground support. The ESA hopes that will generate more data on any ocular degeneration, and possibly provide early warning signs that changes in the eye may be occurring—even before they result in vision change.

Other technical challenges include getting around using batteries to power the device because they pose such a big fire risk. In spacecraft, where space is at a premium, designers will also have to decide where the binocular-sized equipment would live and how to position and keep an astronaut’s head in place without gravity (typically, that’s done by having a chin rest).

But that’s a walk-in-the-park compared with getting a retiree whose sight is failing to cooperate, says Allen. “We're very confident, because we're trying to do that with 80-year-old patients who already have some level of visual imparity,” says Allen, “whereas these will be highly trained astronauts who are much younger and have full function of their eyes.”

”I think lots of the stuff that we're doing for space will bleed through and make our home device better, and vice versa as well,” he adds. “All this research and development work, in principle, is making our products that are going to go into the NHS much better.”

entries.title: The Complicated Case of Passing On Your Digital Estate
entries.summary: There’s no perfect way to transfer possession of your digital assets to your loved ones after you’re gone. But there are things you can do now to make the process easier for them.
entries.content:
When a loved one dies, who downloads their important files from their cloud storage account? Who monitors their email inbox? Who decides what happens to the photos and videos on their social media accounts? And what if those tasks fall to you?

Everyone will die, but not everyone has planned what they want to happen with their digital assets after they're gone. Even when someone makes a plan, survivors might still be limited in what they can do.

Tying up loose ends can become a nightmare for the living, especially when the volume of digital assets is enormous. Still, the more you know, the better you can plan for your own digital estate, and the easier it will be to manage someone else's.

Take Inventory

The biggest determining factor in how much work it’s going to be to manage the online accounts and digital assets of someone who is incapacitated or deceased is whether they did any estate planning. If a person doesn't write down what digital assets they have and what they want done with them, it's impossible for anyone to know.

It's not always a simple matter of memorializing a Facebook account or downloading photos from iCloud either. Digital assets can have as much monetary value as sentimental value. Say a person's social media accounts earn dividends. How will a beneficiary collect future proceeds? And should they keep the account alive?

What about cryptocurrency? If it's stored in a private wallet and no one has the key, the money is lost forever. It's a different story, however, if a third party, like Coinbase or PayPal, holds the crypto. At present, bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies are considered “digital assets” and thus need to be treated that way when doing any estate planning.

Navigating the Law

In the US, digital inheritance is overseen by state law, the same as traditional probate and estate matters, according to Benjamin Orzeske, chief counsel at the Uniform Law Commission. He and his organization developed a state law known as the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA), which has been enacted in 48 states, Washington, DC, and the US Virgin Islands. The missing two states are Massachusetts, where RUFADAA has been adopted but not yet enacted as of this writing, and Louisiana, which went its own way with a similar but different law.

“At the heart of RUFADAA is this recognition that digital property is in some ways different from traditional, tangible property,” Orzeske says. He gives the example of mail versus email. When a person dies, their mail gets forwarded to a dedicated person, the fiduciary, who then receives incoming communication, bills, and payments. If they get a bill in the mail for a magazine subscription, they know to cancel it. Receiving the mail effectively gives the person appropriate information and access to manage the deceased's accounts and estate going forward. Email is different. The fiduciary doesn't just get new incoming mail. They might also have access to a searchable history of communication, which the deceased person might have expected to be kept private.

The real point of conflict, according to Orzeske, lies in the Stored Communications Act, a federal law that says companies that handle our online assets can't release them without our permission. So RUFADAA gives survivors some rights while retaining the original asset holder's privacy.

Under RUFADAA, a named trusted person can close accounts, but they can only get the contents—meaning the bodies of emails, private messages, videos, photos, attachments, and so forth—if the decedent specifically “grants the authority to the personal representative fiduciary,” according to Catherine Hodder, a senior attorney editor at FindLaw. FindLaw is an informational website that breaks down legal issues for a general audience.

The way to give that permission to a trusted person is to write it down, preferably in a will or similar document. Name the person and exactly what you want them to have, but do not list usernames or passwords, Hodder warns, because “the will is a public document.”

If the fiduciary is not given express permission to receive the contents of a digital asset, they might still be able to get a “catalog” of metadata, says Orzeske. Using email as an example again, that could include all the times and dates that emails were sent and received, maybe information about the sender or recipient, but still not the body of emails.

The Shortcomings of Built-In Tools

Many of the big tech companies that hold our digital assets, called “data custodians” in the law, have built-in tools that let you assign a trusted person to access your account when you die or if you become incapacitated.

Google has offered its Inactive Account Manager since 2013. Apple and Meta use the term “legacy contact” in some places, although you have to look for “memorialization” in Instagram. Enabling these features may seem like the easiest way to pass on your accounts, but in practice, the features leave much to be desired.

For example, if you want to give someone permission to download your Instagram content after you die, that person must also have an Instagram account. More importantly, someone must still reach out to Instagram to declare that a person has died in the first place. And how do you do that?

Mike Kiser, a co-chair of the Death in the Digital Estate Community Group at the OpenID Foundation, points out that “there is no defined way to tell a provider that someone has died or lost capacity.” His group has the long-term goal of developing protocols and guidance for users to be able to manage their digital estates.

Other hurdles and unforeseen problems crop up on a case-by-case basis. What happens if you never gave your real name or real date of birth to any of these companies? How can your trusted contact prove that an online account was actually held by you?

Even DIY Solution Can End in Failure

Tech-savvy people have long hacked together do-it-yourself solutions for passing on their digital estates. Some leave a printed document in a secure place listing all their accounts and credentials to get into them. Some leverage the legacy tools in a password manager, which is one of the better options in terms of security, but even the best solutions can come up short.

Kiser says that one of his colleagues created a DIY system for passing on his assets and decided to test it from the point of view of his trusted person. “He failed in step one,” Kiser says.

While researching this story, I experimented with my digital estate and realized that my two-factor authentication app is protected by biometrics. So even if my trusted person had all my credentials via a password manager, they couldn't get very far without my fingerprint.

There's also the sticky issue of violating a data custodian's terms of service, which is likely what happens when someone other than you logs into your accounts. Whether a company would ever press charges is another matter, though it's not hard to imagine times when they might, like when celebrities and public figures are involved.

A more likely scenario is that loved ones disagree about how to handle a decedent's assets and accounts. If the wishes are written out in a will, family in-fighting might still take place, but the fiduciary at least has legal protection.

One other possibility is to create a local backup of all your data that someone can easily open. Send everything to a USB drive, leave it unencrypted, and voilà. Of course, you'll have to regularly export and back up everything you want included, and it doesn't solve the problem of terminating any online accounts you want closed after you're gone.

What’s Best for Now?

Although every solution is imperfect, the best option seems to be naming a fiduciary or a trusted person in your will, then writing your specific wishes in that will or in a similar legal document, where you should be as detailed as possible. List the accounts and digital assets you have, name the person or people who should get them, and describe exactly what they should do.

If you go that route, remember to keep your list of passwords and login credentials separate; only share those with the specific people who need them. Also, do not enable those legacy features in your online accounts. According to Kiser, a platform’s own online controls take top priority and thus could override what you put into your instructions.

Most important of all, update your final instructions documents regularly, like whenever you make any changes to your accounts or move assets around.

entries.title: 4 Best Compression Boots: Therabody, Hyperice, and More (2026)
entries.summary: Whether you’re training hard, traveling often, or dealing with poor circulation, these are the best compression boots for anyone looking for better muscle recovery.
entries.content:
The appeal of compression boots is easy to understand: After an intense workout or a long run, these sleeves wrap around your legs and mimic the squeezing sensation of a massage. The sequential air pressure is meant to treat delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and improve circulation, helping blood, oxygen, and nutrients through tired muscles.

Unlike many wellness gadgets that make big promises with little evidence behind them, intermittent pneumatic compression has been used for decades in medical and rehabilitation settings. Today, brands like Hyperice and Therabody have created at-home systems designed for everyone from marathon runners to workers who spend long hours on their feet.

But with prices ranging from a few hundred to well over $1,000—like our top pick, the Therabody JetBoots Pro Plus—and add-ons like heat and red light therapy, it can be difficult to know which boots are worth the investment. I tested the best compression boots to find the models that deliver the ideal combination of comfort, performance, and customization.

For more muscle recovery tools, check out our guides to the Best Massage Guns, Best Massagers, and Best Therabody Devices.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Featured in This Guide

Best Compression Boots Overall

The Therabody JetBoots Pro Plus are the most feature-packed recovery boots I tested, combining pneumatic compression, vibrations, and infrared LED light therapy in one wireless system.

Why WIRED recommends: The compression and vibrating pairing is therapeutic, to say the least; it consistently left my legs feeling less stiff after workouts. Everything is controlled from an LCD screen built into the lead boot, so there’s no separate controller to keep track of. You can tailor every session to your preference, with durations ranging from 10 to 60 minutes in five-minute increments and manual controls to adjust both pressure—measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg)—and vibration intensity. You can also choose from four compression modes and eight preset routines.

The trade-offs: Therabody doesn’t publish key specs about the LEDs, and I didn’t notice a significant difference in my post-workout recovery that I could attribute to the infrared light therapy. The boots also don’t connect to the Therabody app, which may disappoint some users, but I didn’t find it necessary. At $1,150, these are also among the priciest compression boots on the market.

Buy if: You want the most premium, customizable recovery system available and don’t mind the splurge. They’re especially suited for athletes and anyone who exercises regularly, or for people managing conditions like lymphedema, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), or chronic venous insufficiency (CVI).

Specs
Compression 20–100 mmHg in 5-minute and 5-mmHg increments
Sizes (Leg Length) Short: 27 to 32 inches; Regular: 32 to 37 inches; Long: 37+ inches
Weight Short: 11.3 pounds; Regular: 12.4 pounds; Long: 12.8 pounds
Battery Life 150 to 240 minutes
Warranty 1 year

Best Entry-Level Compression Boots

If all you want is effective pneumatic compression, the Therabody JetBoots Prime delivers the essentials at a more affordable price point.

Why WIRED recommends: For half the cost of the JetBoots Pro Plus, the Prime skips the vibration and infrared LED therapies but still offers four compression levels (25, 50, 75, and 100 mmHg) and three session lengths (20, 40, or 60 minutes), all controlled from a built-in panel on the boot. They’re wireless compression boots, offer up to three hours of battery life, and can even be used while charging. Weighing about 6 pounds, they’re surprisingly portable and fold down into the included drawstring backpack.

The trade-offs: Customization is limited compared to pricier models. While the boots are foldable, they’re still bulky enough that squeezing them into the drawstring bag can be a bit of a hassle.

Buy if: You want an affordable, no-frills pair of compression boots that nail the basics. They’re a great choice for first-time buyers or anyone who doesn’t want the extras like vibration or red-light therapy.

Specs
Compression 25–100 mmHg in 25-mmHg increments
Sizes (Leg Length) Short: 27 to 32 inches; Regular: 32 to 37 inches; Long: 37+ inches
Weight Short: 5.5 pounds; Regular: 6 pounds; Long: 6.3 pounds
Battery Life ~180 minutes
Warranty 1 year

Best Portable Compression Boots

If you want the recovery benefits of compression therapy without investing in full-length boots, the Normatec Go is the easiest system to live with.

Why WIRED recommends: These calf sleeves ditch the hoses and external control unit in favor of a wearable design. You can recover while making dinner, working from home, or walking around the airport. Each sleeve delivers 360-degree dynamic air compression across three overlapping zones with seven intensity levels. They’re compact, TSA-approved, and light enough to pack in a carry-on or personal item. They’re also compatible with the Hyperice app.

The trade-offs: Since the Normatec Go only targets your calves, you won’t get the full leg compression that traditional boots provide. They also don’t include a storage case, which feels like a necessity for a product designed to be portable.

Buy if: You travel frequently, want a recovery device you can use on the go, or are looking to reduce calf fatigue without packing a full-size pair of recovery boots.

Specs
Compression 7 levels of compression (40–200 mmHg)
Weight 1.2 pounds
Battery Life Up to 3 hours
Warranty 1 year

Best Compression Therapy for Hips

Most compression systems focus on your legs, but the Normatec Elite Hips targets your hips and glutes, which are just as prone to tightness.

Why WIRED recommends: Two overlapping air pumps deliver even, consistent pressure across your hips, glutes, IT bands, and lower back, without leaving noticeable gaps in coverage. They feature seven intensity levels, making it just as useful for loosening up after a long run as it is for activating your hips before a workout. The Elite Hips are also wireless and offer up to four hours of battery life.

The trade-offs: They’re not a replacement for compression boots. While they provide some relief to your upper quads and hamstrings, their primary focus is the hips and glutes.

Buy if: You regularly struggle with tight hips after activities like running or cycling, or you want to improve hip mobility and range of motion. They’re also worth considering if you’re looking for a noninvasive remedy to help manage conditions like sciatica or hip arthritis—just be sure to consult your health care provider first.

Specs
Compression 7 levels of compression (40–110 mmHg)
Weight 3.4 pounds
Battery Life Up to 4 hours
Warranty 1 year

Compare Top 4 Compression Boots

Product Coverage Compression Weight Battery Life FSA/HSA Eligible Price

Therabody JetBoots Prime Foot to thigh 25–100 mmHg in 25-mmHg increments Short: 5.5 pounds; Regular: 6 pounds; Long: 6.3 pounds ~180 minutes Yes $550
Hyperice Normatec Go Calves 7 levels of compression (40–110 mmHg) 1.2 pounds Up to 3 hours Yes $379
Hyperice Normatec Elite Hips Hips, glutes, lower back, upper IT bands 7 levels of compression (40–110 mmHg) 3.4 pounds Up to 4 hours Yes $599

Honorable Mentions

Hyperboot by Nike × Hyperice for $799: These high-top, sneaker-like foot massagers combine targeted air compression and heat therapy for your heels and ankles, letting you move around while recovering. That said, WIRED contributor Kristin Canning found the arch support lacking and the battery life short (roughly 60 to 90 minutes), so she wouldn’t recommend wearing them for long walks. The ranged sizing also makes it harder to find a secure fit, especially for a product that’s meant to be worn like footwear. At $799, I’d rather invest in a pair of full-length compression boots.

Urevo AI-Powered Wireless Recovery Boots for $780: These compression boots offer a high range of 80 to 180 mmHg; that’s great if you’ve found other options too gentle, but I found the highest settings uncomfortably intense and ultimately counterproductive. Urevo’s companion app offers 32 massage modes tailored to different sports and workouts, which is the most I've seen offered in my testing. These boots also generate AI-powered recovery summaries, though I found them to be pointless. The one-size-fits-most design is another drawback; it accommodates taller users well, but it can feel long if you’re short.

Urevo AI-Powered Wireless Relax Massager for $250: Like the Hyperice Normatec Go, these are calf sleeves, but they incorporate vibrations and heat therapy for a more therapeutic session. Unfortunately, I found the fit constricting and uncomfortably tight once the compression kicked in, which detracted from the overall experience. At their full retail price of $250, I’d still recommend spending a bit more for the Normatec Go. The good news is that they’re almost always on sale. At around $70 (as they were at the time of writing this), they’re an excellent bargain.

What Am I Testing Next?

I'm testing the Hyperice Normatec 3 and the Hyperice Normatec Elite.

entries.title: Meetily Lets You Transcribe and Summarize Meetings Without a Subscription—Here’s How
entries.summary: There are endless ways to record and transcribe your virtual meetings with AI. Here’s an option that’s free and open source.
entries.content:
It's perhaps the least hyped, and most useful, feature of the AI age: transcription. As a young journalist, I dreamed of a computer that could turn recordings into text. Now we have that, and it's amazing.

This tech isn't just great for interviews—it's perfect for meetings. A variety of services, called meeting assistants, promise to transcribe and summarize your meetings for you. The appeal here is obvious, but these services don't come cheap or without privacy concerns. Generally, using them means uploading a recording of your meeting to some cloud somewhere, which isn't ideal for projects that require confidentiality. And the tools themselves are generally in the $10 to $20 per month range, price-wise.

Now, as I pointed out with transcription software, the tech for building something like a meeting assistant is open source and widely available for free. Meetily brings it all together in a simple package. Yes, the name is awful, but it uses open-source models, has a great free version, and is available on Windows and macOS (Linux users can build it from source).

Note that there is a Pro version for $10 per month, but the open-source community version is completely free to download from GitHub. Install the application and it will offer to install the models needed. These are the AI tools that do the actual work.

Once those have downloaded, you will need to allow Meetily to record both your microphone's sound and the system audio—that way it can capture all sides of any conversation you're in.

Then you can hit the record button any time you're in a video call. Accessing your microphone and system sound directly means Meetily isn't restricted to specific videoconferencing tools—it'll work with Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, and any other service you might come across. You can even theoretically use this for an in-person meeting, assuming your laptop's microphone is capable of picking up sound from everyone in the room. (You may want to look at an AI notetaker if you want a separate device.)

During the meeting, you can watch the transcription take place nearly in real time if you want, or minimize the window and focus on your meeting. When the meeting is done, you can click the stop button, at which point you will see a transcription. From here, you can ask for an AI summary. You can even provide instructions about which points to focus on.

Now, as with all AI tools, there are caveats. These systems aren't perfect, and they may not have the same priorities as you. I intend to write my own meeting minutes using the transcript as a guide, but the meeting summary could still prove useful in certain contexts.

A beta feature allows you to use Meetily with recordings you made previously. This means you can drag an audio or even video file and get a transcript and summary. This is useful if you recorded an in-person conversation on your phone, for example, and want to get a transcript when you're back at your computer.

The free version of Meetily has a few annoying limitations. The transcript can't tell you who said what—no speaker labels—which will be a deal-breaker for many people. I could not find a free and open-source tool that did this consistently, though.

There are a few other similar tools out there if Meetily doesn't work for you. For example, noScribe is a completely free tool that can identify speakers, though it can't record meetings in real time (it only converts files). Anarlog (formerly known as Hyprnote) has an arguably sleeker user interface and access to many AI models, but setup was a bit fiddly compared to Meetily. Quill offers free local transcriptions, but you'll need to sign up for an account to use it (which defeats the point of an offline tool), and there's a lot of upselling.

It's great there are so many free options, and if this field is anything like dictation software, I'm sure there will be even more in a few months.

entries.title: TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper Review (2026): A Hybrid Tablet for Taking Notes and Watching Video
entries.summary: TCL’s hybrid tablet-digital notebook tries to be the best of both worlds, and it mostly succeeds.
entries.content:
Nice high-res matte screen. Excellent pen with good pressure sensitivity. Good handwriting conversion tools. Works well as an ebook reader. Great for watching video.

TIRED

Keyboard case adds unnecessary bulk. Lacks hardware volume buttons. User interface feels like a work in progress. Writing onscreen isn't as nice as on E Ink devices.

Tablets are secondary devices for most of us, but there's one place where they outshine laptops: digital note-taking. Attempting to bridge the gap between analog and digital, digital notebooks offer a paper-like writing experience with all the pros of digital notes.

ReMarkable devices are probably the best known in this space, and they top our digital notebook guide, but I've always wanted something a little more versatile—what if I want to stream a baseball game on the same device I take notes on? E Ink, the technology employed by digital notebooks and e-readers, isn't the best choice in that case.

TCL's Note A1 Nxtpaper tablet uses a more traditional, though still matte, tablet screen to get as close to the E Ink writing experience as possible, while still being able to display video when you want to expand beyond just taking notes. It mostly works, but it can't completely mimic the feel of writing on paper, and there are a few quirks with the user interface.

Hybrid Screen

The heart of any digital notebook is the screen—how well does it mimic paper? With E Ink, the answer is pretty darn well, but this is not actually E Ink. TCL's Note A1 Nxtpaper is built around a custom 1440 x 2200-pixel matte LCD panel with a 120-Hz refresh rate. At first glance, it looks like E Ink, and indeed it reduces glare and is easier on the eye than a typical tablet. At the same time, it's still an LCD panel capable of the color rendering and responsiveness of a traditional Android tablet. (The Nxtpaper matte LCD technology is proprietary to TCL.)

It's not E Ink, but I find the Note A1 screen to be quite nice and a perfectly acceptable alternative given how much more versatile it is than an E Ink screen. However, if what you love about E Ink note-taking devices is the paperlike experience, this is not the device for you (I'll explain more in the next section). It's certainly much nicer to look at and to write on than a typical glossy Android tablet.

While it is not perfect, the Note A1's screen feels very close to the hybrid note-taking/true tablet device that I've been searching for—one part real screen, one part writing pad.

The rest of the tablet is about what you'd expect in a midrange to high-end Android tablet. There's a MediaTek G100 processor, with 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. That's enough power to run all the apps I tested and power some of the AI-driven features TCL is pushing with this device, including automated meeting summaries, audio-to-text transcription, and, of course, handwriting-to-text conversion.

All this is wrapped in a solid aluminum body that's almost exactly the same size and weight as the 11-inch Kindle Scribe. The Note A1 is 5 millimeters thick and weighs 500 grams.

I have two gripes with the Note A1 hardware. The first is the keyboard case, which is unnecessarily heavy and complicated. TCL apparently hired an origami expert to design the keyboard case, which has three panels where two usually does the job. The result is a keyboard case that adds an annoying level of weight, thickness, and complexity where none of that is required. For all that though, the keyboard itself is quite nice to type on. The other problem is the lack of hardware volume buttons. Volume buttons are good, mmmkay?

Writing, Drawing, Reading

Besides the screen, the bundled T-Pen Pro is the highlight of this tablet. The fact that it's bundled is somewhat unusual these days, as many manufacturers have followed Apple's lead and made their writing devices a separate purchase.

This isn't some throwaway pen either; it's very good, with excellent pressure sensitivity and extremely low latency, which makes writing with it feel a lot more natural than some tablets I've tested.

But the overall writing experience doesn't feel like paper. Devices like the ReMarkable have spent a lot of effort getting the texture and feel of paper into the screen-writing experience. The A1 Note can't compete on this front because it still feels like writing on a glass tablet. This didn't bother me as I've never really wanted to replicate the exact feel of paper notebooks on digital (if I want to write on paper, I, well, write on paper), but if you're coming from a device like the ReMarkable, know that the writing experience here is more like a traditional tablet screen.

Despite this, the pen is really nice for taking notes, annotating documents, and even sketching. There are several tips available, and you can customize the pen quite a bit, including setting up custom shortcuts. There's also good handwriting and shape recognition tools in the A1 Note's note-taking software.

The Note A1 supports a broad range of document formats, from PDF docs to Word, PowerPoint, Excel, EPUB, MOBI, AZW3 (Kindle), and more. That means you aren't locked into any specific reader or app on the device.

Similarly for syncing, you can use whatever you like. TCL ships with Google's Play Store installed, but I had no trouble downloading and installing F-Droid, then installing Syncthing and some open-source apps that I use. That said, at times, I felt like I was fighting against the UI that TCL developed for the Note A1.

The device, despite running Android, has a UI designed for note-taking. There's a sidebar that gives you access to any apps you install (more on that below). At the top of the screen is a short to-do list and the Inspiration Space, which is like a free-form clipboard area where you can store things you want to highlight (pretty much anything, which is very useful). Below that, you have your list of notes.

Click on a note with the pen, and it will open in edit mode with a configuration toolbar shown across the top. Here you can set up pen type, color, line thickness, and all the other tools you'd want to use to write or draw. I found the editing interface just about perfect in the sense that it balances keeping it simple but still giving you access to the controls you actually need.

The other element I enjoyed in the Note A1 UI is the Inspiration Space. I can easily clip a bit of text from any document (including web pages), save it, and then automatically convert it to text for use in something else or apply any of the other onboard AI-powered tools. It's one of the best clip-and-save tools I've used since I gave up on Evernote.

What I was less thrilled with is the file management system. It works, but there are confusing shortcomings. For example, I couldn't find a way to open a note in reading mode and then switch to editing from within the note. This seems like a very common use case. But no, you have to exit the note, go back to the main notes menu, and then reopen it in editing mode.

The interface is not very intuitive. I had to consult the manual to figure out how to get two documents open side-by-side, something that works by drag and drop in every other Android device I've tested (even those with highly customized UIs).

A Note on Earlier Versions

Curiously for a large publicly traded company, TCL launched the Note A1 via Kickstarter (but clearly already had plenty of the tablet available, which the company fed to YouTube influencers). If you hunt down early reviews of these Kickstarter devices, you'll notice people complaining about limited app availability, no Google Play Store, and having to sideload apps via F-Droid, the Aurora Store, and other shenanigans.

The Note A1 I tested, and the device that is for sale these days at all major retailers, comes with the Google Play Store preinstalled, making it easy to download any app you need. Accessing installed apps can be a little awkward; they pile up in the sidebar menu, but if you make good use of the ability to customize the launcher, it's not too difficult to have everything you need close at hand. And for completeness sake, I did install F-Droid and the Aurora Store, and both also work (although if Google carries through with its current development plans for Android, apps installed with F-Droid will stop working on all Android devices next year).

Competition

There are two competitors here. The first is an E Ink tablet. If you want the most paperlike possible experience, then the E Ink wins. But you won't be watching videos or perusing social media. If you want 80 percent of the E Ink experience, but also the ability to use your device as a normal Android tablet, then the Note A1 is the clear winner.

The other major competitor here is TCL itself, namely the Nxtpaper 11 Plus, which offers much of the same experience, albeit with a less powerful chip, costs half the price, and doesn't have the same custom UI. Most compellingly, the Nxtpaper 11 Plus is regularly on sale for less than half the price of the Note A1 Nxtpaper. While you do get a nicer, more powerful piece of hardware in the Note A1, I'm not sure it's twice as nice.

While the Note A1 is not perfect, for the right person it's pretty close. The screen is excellent and paperlike enough for most people, and writing and drawing are great. The keyboard, though deeply flawed, works fine, while the software is 90 percent of the way there; encouragingly, TCL seems to be updating it based on feedback. As with all TCL devices, the support period is on the short side, but given the level of Android customization here, I don't think that's unreasonable. If you've been looking for an E Ink–like device that's more versatile, this is the best hybrid tablet I've tested.

Scott Gilbertson is Operations Manager for the WIRED Reviews Team. He was previously a writer and editor for WIRED’s Webmonkey.com, covering the independent web and early internet culture. You can reach him at luxagraf.net. ... Read More

entries.title: The 12 Best Anime to Watch if You Think You Hate Anime
entries.summary: Japan’s strongest media export makes a solid case for your attention span. Here’s what to watch.
entries.content:
Despite its ferocious popularity, people still tend to swear off anime entirely. These are usually the people whose reference of the medium pertains to a certain stereotype or to the few seconds of anime they once saw on a computer somewhere in the early 2000s.

But Japan has been producing some of the most emotionally resonant and visually audacious storytelling in contemporary media for half a century, and a great deal of it looks nothing at all like the stereotype it holds.

So here’s a case for the uninitiated. Start with self-contained films you can knock out in a single evening before graduating to series worth committing wholly to. The common thread, if you’re keeping score, is that not one of these requires you to know anything about anime, or Japan for that matter, going in.

Note that many of these picks are available in both the original Japanese audio with subtitles or as “dubs” with dialog dubbed by English voice actors. Dive in however you’d like.

Solo Leveling

If you want something fast, slick and unapologetically addictive, start here. Adapted from a South Korean web novel and webtoon by the Japanese animation studio A-1 Pictures, Solo Leveling follows Sung Jinwoo, an E-rank hunter regarded as the weakest of his profession. After being slaughtered during a dungeon expedition, he awakens with access to a mysterious system that only he can see–and which allows him to become stronger in a world where everyone else’s abilities are effectively fixed. Watching him transform from expendable underdog into an overwhelmingly powerful fighter is pure wish fulfillment, driven by propulsive pacing and enormous battles.

The Girl Who Leapt Through Time

This 2006 film is one of the softest possible landings into anime, with a concept that is simple to follow. Makoto is an ordinary teenager who unexpectedly discovers that she can leap backward through time. She initially uses the ability to redo poor test results, avoid awkward confessions, and correct everyday embarrassments. But manipulating time has consequences for the people around her, forcing Makoto to confront a future she may not be able to reverse.

Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End

Most fantasy stories end when the heroes defeat the great evil. Frieren begins there. After completing a decade-long quest, the elven mage takes off on a solitary journey, returning after 50 years to find that her human companions have aged while she has remained unchanged. Regret at missing out on reconnecting earlier and the pain of witnessing the death of one of her friends sets her on a journey of self-discovery. The result is a quiet, beautifully animated meditation on memory, mortality, and the meaning we find in seemingly fleeting relationships.

Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind

Take a trip back to the anime of the ’80s, when writer-director Hayao Miyazaki was helping redefine what Japanese animation could accomplish—even before he cofounded Studio Ghibli. Set in a world poisoned by ecological catastrophe, the film follows Princess Nausicaä as she tries to prevent a war between human kingdoms while understanding the enormous toxic forest spreading across the planet. It is a postapocalyptic adventure but also a remarkably prescient story about environmental destruction and humanity’s impulse to conquer what it fears.

Death Note

For viewers who think anime means sprawling fights and exaggerated superpowers, Death Note offers a psychological thriller instead. High school student Light Yagami discovers a supernatural notebook that allows him to kill anyone whose name he writes inside it, provided he knows their face. With this discovery, he launches a crusade to eliminate criminals. What follows is a compulsive, morally murky battle of wits about justice, power, and how quickly idealism can become tyranny.

The Colors Within

Totsuko is a Catholic girls’ school student with an ability to see people’s emotions as colors. She joins a band with two people whose auras she’s drawn to, and so unfolds a musical odyssey of emotion and connection, tuned to classic anime characteristics. This 2024 Japanese drama film is a great watch if you’re after something with a bit more depth.

Jujutsu Kaisen

For anyone who wants supernatural horror with spectacular action, Jujutsu Kaisen is an easy gateway. High school student Yuji Itadori swallows a cursed finger to save a classmate and becomes the vessel of Ryomen Sukuna, a reincarnated sorcerer known as the King of Curses. Yuji is brought into the secretive world of jujutsu sorcerers, who fight supernatural beings created from humanity’s negative emotions. The series becomes considerably darker as it progresses, but its humor, memorable characters, and inventive battles make the commitment worthwhile.

The Tale of the Princess Kaguya

Japan’s most famous folklore reimagined in a hand-drawn masterpiece by Isao Takahata took eight years to make. As if sketched in real time, the story unfolds with a bamboo cutter who discovers a tiny girl inside a stalk. He raises her and watches her transform into a woman of impossible beauty. But the girl is slowly suffocated by everyone else’s plans for her, including five noble suitors competing for her hand.

Kiki’s Delivery Service

Even if you have never explored anime, you have probably encountered this one. Hayao Miyazaki’s 1989 fantasy follows Kiki, a 13-year-old witch who leaves home as part of her training and settles in a seaside city with her talking cat, Jiji. She begins supporting herself by running an airborne delivery service, only to find her confidence—and her ability to fly—beginning to disappear. Ostensibly a children’s film, it is also an unusually perceptive story about independence, loneliness, and creative burnout.

Spirited Away

Hayao Miyazaki’s 2001 masterpiece remains one of the strongest arguments for animation as serious cinema. Ten-year-old Chihiro unknowingly enters a mysterious spirit world where her parents eat food at an abandoned amusement park and are transformed into pigs. She then finds work in a magical bathhouse as she searches for a way to save them.

Strange, frightening, and intensely imaginative, the film refuses to explain every corner of its world. Instead, it trusts viewers to follow Chihiro through a story about courage, greed and growing up. In 2003, it became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature.

Fruits Basket

Developed from its Japanese manga origin to a full animated series in 2019, Fruits Basket is a wild story of a generational curse spanning three seasons. The Soma family has a strange secret. If any of them embrace, they transform into animals of the Chinese zodiac. By its final season, it earns catharsis as much as it does a fanbase of emotionally invested devotees. Hulu has the English dubbed version, and Crunchyroll has both the dubbed and subtitled versions.

Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba

If you find yourself somewhat tempted by anime that’s got swords and demons, this is an adventure series for you. It is also one of the biggest animation phenomenons of the decade, with movie spinoffs that have broken box office records. Main character Tanjiro embarks on a wild journey to avenge a demon attack on his family, unfolding over four seasons of thrilling plot lines and impressive hand-drawn fight sequences.

This story was originally published by WIRED Middle East.

entries.title: 8 Best Workout Headphones & Earbuds: Beats, Bose, Apple (2026)
entries.summary: Not every great pair of headphones belongs in the gym. These do, thanks to their secure fit, durable design, and impeccable sound.
entries.content:
The best workout headphones disappear when you start moving. They’re locked in without readjustments and comfortable enough that the music feels like it’s coming from inside your head. Your workout headphones have a tougher job than your everyday pair. They need to survive sweat, being thrown into a gym bag, and the occasional drop. They also need to sound good enough to keep you motivated until the finish line.

The WIRED Reviews team has tested hundreds of headphones and earbuds, and I’ve narrowed down the models that best balance sound quality, comfort, and durability. We put these picks through workouts like weightlifting and indoor swimming, as well as outdoor activities like trail runs, hikes, and cycling, to evaluate which headphones enhanced the experience and which ones got in the way. This roundup includes a mix of headphones and earbuds, wired and wireless, from the top pick, the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 ($250), to the bone-conduction Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 ($180).

For more recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, the Best Open Earbuds, and the Best Bone Conduction Headphones.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Featured in This Guide

Best Wireless Earbuds for Working Out

Beats were the first sport earbuds to tap into Apple’s ecosystem, but the Powerbeats Pro 2 work nearly as well with Android, making them a great pick for any phone. The redesigned nickel-titanium ear hooks stayed in place through hours of testing, and former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata said they’re the most comfortable hooked earbuds he’s worn. The noise canceling is a major upgrade, outperforming the Beats Studio Buds+ and holding its own against premium rivals like Sony’s WF-1000XM5 and Technics’ AZ80. The Powerbeats Pro 2 also finally add a natural-sounding transparency mode, along with punchy sound, up to 10 hours of battery life (eight with ANC enabled), and convenient push-button controls.

Apple users get extras like iCloud device switching, Find My functionality, and hands-free Siri, while Android users still benefit from the Beats app, heart rate monitoring, and one-touch pairing. I wish the PowerBeats Pro 2 had a higher IP rating than IPX4, but they’re still built to handle sweat and light rain.

Specs
Battery Life Up to 10 hours (8 hours with ANC enabled; Case holds an extra 35 hours)
Durability IPX4
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Wireless Headphones for Working Out

If you prefer over-ear headphones for your workouts, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 are hard to beat. The plush fit is comfortable enough for long listening sessions, and the impressive noise canceling blocks out any distractions at the gym. The sound is clear and engaging, with plenty of punch, plus a transparency mode that feels natural. Bose also added useful upgrades like USB-C lossless audio, improved ambient controls, and longer battery life.

The ear cups do trap heat and sweat, but I have yet to find a pair of over-ear headphones that don't encourage sweat during intense workouts. Nonetheless, they are a premium pick for anyone who wants workout headphones to double as everyday headphones.

Specs
Battery Life Up to 30 hours
Durability No IP rating
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Budget Buds

JLab’s Go Air Sport is the sport version of the insanely affordable Go Air, with a slight markup for over-ear hooks and a case with a cover. That case also has a built-in USB charger. The build quality is solid, and touch controls are not too sensitive; I don't accidentally turn off my music or turn up the volume whenever I adjust my hair or my hat. They have a solid 30 hours of battery life when you recharge them in the case. I wore them for two weeks for a few hours each day while running and walking my dog, and I didn't have to recharge them once. And the Bluetooth connection is stronger than most affordable earbuds I've tried; I don't have to be wary about walking around a corner, away from my phone. As a bonus, they also come in a wide array of playful colors. —Adrienne So

Specs
Battery Life Up to 35 hours
Durability IP55
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Premium Earbuds

Bose is the undisputed king of noise-canceling headphones, so if you really need to lock in, consider the QuietComfort Ultra 2 Earbuds. According to former editor Parker Hall, the noise-canceling on the second-gen pair bested the competition and was better than its predecessor. You get wireless charging in the clamshell and guards to prevent earwax buildup. Bose uses a chiming calibration tool to adjust the sound profile and noise-canceling response to the shape of your actual ear canals, which is impressive. If you get too deep in the zone, there's also an Aware mode that lets you hear ambient noise while smoothing out loud sounds. Not only are these the best for the gym, but they're also probably the best pair for anyone who wants noise cancellation in a compact package that you can tote around every day. —Adrienne So

Specs
Battery Life Up to 30 hours
Durability IPX4
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Earbuds for Apple Users

The AirPods Pro 3 are the first AirPods model I've used that I legitimately consider to be workout headphones. (Previous models fell out all the time.) Apple conducted what former WIRED editor Parker Hall calls “an ungodly number” of laser ear scans, and there is a greater choice of ear tips. The XXS small tips actually fit me well, and these are the first AirPods Pros that haven't fallen out of my ears while running.

Like the Powerbeats Pro 2, they also have heart rate sensing, so if you're tracking your workout with Fitness+ and using Workout Buddy, you can see your live heart rate in the app or on your Apple Watch. Noise canceling is also excellent if you're working out in the gym. Apple's bass-heavy, bright tuning is also ideal if you're bopping around to pop sensations like Haim or Mariah Carey when you're working out. —Adrienne So

Specs
Battery Life Up to 8 hours with ANC, 24 hours with the case
Durability IPX4
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Earbuds for Running

The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 now charge via USB-C, so you can say goodbye to their proprietary charger. These earbuds use both air and bone conduction to transmit sound while you’re working out outside. This new model added a second air-conduction unit, which improves the sound quality and reduces the tingling sensation you get with bone conduction.

WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Sawh notes that the battery life is slightly less than promised, and the waterproof rating is lower than on previous iterations (IP67). According to Sawh, the sound quality isn’t as clear as one might like, but the bass and punch are still powerful. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So says these are her favorite pair of headphones for cycling because they fit comfortably underneath a helmet.

Specs
Battery Life Up to 12 hours
Durability IP55
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Earbuds for Swimming

The OpenSwim Pro has an industry-leading IP68 rating and a dedicated swimming EQ mode that produces a balanced sound that is pleasant to listen to underwater. According to WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Sawh, the controls are easy to use, and the neckband is slim enough to wear under a swim cap. Since Bluetooth doesn’t work underwater, you’ll need to import audio files from your computer onto your swim headphones. There’s 32 GB of onboard storage. Be sure to check the format to make sure it's compatible; the OpenSwim Pro supports MP3, FLAC, WAV, AAC, M4A, APE, and WMA files.

Specs
Battery Life Up to 9 hours
Durability IP68
Compatibility iOS and Android

Best Wired Earbuds for Working Out

If you're running or hiking, it's convenient to have a pair of earbuds that are attached to you and won't fall into a puddle. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these Soundpeats Q40HD, mainly because they’re designed with two clips to attach to your shirt; plus the buds themselves are magnetic and click together when not in use. In testing, Adrienne was able to get around 20 hours of battery life, and even when power is low, a quick top-off with a USB-C cable got her more than enough battery to last for an hour-long trail run. The headphones don't include active noise cancellation, but they fit well enough to provide passive noise cancellation. They block ambient sounds so well, in fact, that she only wears one bud when running.

Specs
Battery Life Up to 20 hours
Durability IP67
Compatibility iOS and Android

Honorable Mentions

BlueAnt Pump X for $100: The BlueAnt Pump X has an incredible standout feature: cooling gel ear pads that you can keep in the fridge and swap out for the regular ear pads, so you don't get too sweaty. The single-button operation is intuitive, and ANC is effective. Battery life was also startlingly long—I wore them for an hour or two a day for several weeks before the battery got to 50 percent. The regular ear pads are soft and comfortable, and they're also water-resistant, which is unusual in over-ear gym headphones. There's also a special X Mode that pumps up the bass; I could feel distinct vibrations with my bass standard, Beyoncé's “Partition.” The price is also reasonable. —Adrienne So

Skullcandy Crusher 540 Active for $210: The BlueAnt headphones are just a better buy in all regards, but I enjoyed these a lot. The noise canceling doesn't work very well, but these headphones are attractive, and the bass is powerful. —Adrienne So

Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro’s sound quality is excellent; the buds are beautiful and comfortable; and I appreciate the physical buttons. That said, the open-ear noise-reduction system merely blunts outside noise rather than blocking it, so I don't understand the value here. —Adrienne So

Soundcore AeroFit 2 Pro for $180: The AeroFit 2 Pro physically switches modes with its adjustable ear hooks to transform from open earbuds to noise-canceling ones. Unfortunately, I found the case to be too big, and the noise cancellation wasn’t so effective. Still, it's an interesting concept, and I do like being able to toggle the angle on the ear hooks for a more secure fit. —Adrienne So

Oakley Meta Vanguard for $499: Not only are they Oakley sunglasses with Prizm lenses for enhancing contrast and keeping you from tumbling head over heels on the trail, but they also have a 12-MP action camera in the bridge of the nose, two over-ear speakers with a five-mic array for calls, and they integrate with Garmin to work as a (not very useful) fitness tracker. That's OK, because these are the best for moving at speed. They are 6 decibels louder than the Oakley Meta HSTNs, and you can tell. They're the only open headphones where I don't have to turn the volume all the way up to hear podcasts when going over 20 mph. —Adrienne So

Chamelo Music Shield for $260: Chamelo's audio sunglasses have electro-chromic lenses; you can change how dark they get with a finger slider on the arm. However, the music isn't very loud, the battery life is much worse than the Vanguard, and they're relatively expensive. —Adrienne So

JLab Epic Sport ANC 3 for $100: This is the upgraded version of the Go Air Sport above, with hybrid dual drivers for better sound, a higher IP rating, better battery life, and active noise canceling. You need a fully sealed fit for ANC to be effective, which these don't have; I can still hear people at the gym when I'm lifting weights. Still, in every other way, these headphones meet their promises, and they do feel secure. —Adrienne So

H2O Audio Tri 2 Pro Multi-Sport for $220: These are a huge improvement from the first iteration of the brand's waterproof headphones, thanks to a more secure fit, better buttons, and a smoother silicone finish. However, they're pricier than the Shokz, and they use a proprietary charger instead of USB-C. —Adrienne So

Nwm Go for $99: Stylish Japanese brand Nwm recently launched these open-ear bone conduction headphones that purport to reduce sound leakage. It works—they sound fine and are incredibly light; they also use a proprietary charger. —Adrienne So

Nothing Open Earbuds for $99: These are some of the slimmest buds I've tested, and they fit well under layers of hoods, helmets, and hats. —Adrienne So

JLab JBuds Mini for $40: For tiny earbuds, these sound pretty decent. They’re IP55, so they’re sweatproof and dustproof, and because they fit so well, the noise canceling is effective. The biggest drawback is that they’re not great for phone calls. They also only get around five hours of playtime without the case and 20 hours with it.

Suunto Sonic for $79: If you want to try a neckband-style headphone like the Shokz above, but for cheaper, WIRED contributor Michael Sawh says these are lightweight with a balanced sound profile. —Adrienne So

Speck Gemtones Sport for $70: These are cheap and fit well. The buttons are a little too sensitive, and the sound is noticeably fuzzier than most of our other picks, but they're not terrible. —Adrienne So

Avoid These Headphones and Earbuds

Raycon Bone Conduction Headphones for $100: These headphones were so uncomfortable, pressing on my ear canal where they buzzed the flesh of my eardrums and not my bones. It was unbearable. —Adrienne So

Skullcandy Method 360 ANC for $130: In testing, I found the earbuds and case to be huge. The noise canceling also doesn’t work at all. —Adrienne So

Anker Soundcore C40i for $120: These open-ear buds fell out before I'd run a block down my street. I put them in my pocket and didn't wear them again for the rest of the run. —Adrienne So

1More Fit Open for $55: These earbuds sound OK, but the buttons are so sensitive that I couldn't run for more than five minutes without a song skipping or the music turning off. —Adrienne So

entries.title: These AI Barons Are Ready to Give Away Their Fortunes
entries.summary: A new generation of philanthropists made rich by artificial intelligence are preparing to give away their vast wealth. What should we make of a multi-billion-dollar pinky promise?
entries.content:
David Silver is a billionaire, sort of. His stake in Ineffable Intelligence—the artificial intelligence lab he founded—is worth an ungodly fortune. But he stands to collect none of that money himself. He set things up that way.

Between 2013 and 2025, Silver worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He specialized in reinforcement learning, a method of teaching an AI model through positive and negative feedback. In 2016, he led the development of AlphaGo, which became the first AI to defeat a human champion in the game of Go and was heralded as a narrow form of superintelligence. Silver left to start Ineffable Intelligence in January, betting that reinforcement learning breakthroughs will close the gap between human and machine cognition across the board.

When he started Ineffable Intelligence, Silver raised $1.1 billion from investors at a $5.1 billion valuation, reportedly the largest seed round in Europe’s history. He also vowed to donate all the money he makes from any future sale of his company to charity.

“I was thinking very deeply about what I could do to have the maximum impact on the world,” Silver tells WIRED in an interview at his office in Kings Cross, London, around the corner from DeepMind’s headquarters. “Not just through the work I do, but through the finance I arrive at in the process.”

He’ll choose how to deploy the funds after he sells his company, he says, but his ambition is to save as many lives as possible.

Silver is the latest in a growing line of AI founders to pledge equity proceeds to charity. Others include Mustafa Suleyman, a DeepMind cofounder and the CEO of AI at Microsoft, and Anton Osika, the founder of automated coding platform Lovable. If OpenAI and Anthropic go public as planned, minting thousands of new millionaires in the process, the AI industry could soon come to represent an increasingly outsize proportion of tech philanthropy.

Along with a new generation of techno-philanthropists, though, comes a tangle of unresolved questions: Is philanthropy the most appropriate way to redistribute wealth? To what degree are megadonors responsible for some of the problems they aim to fix? Could a pledge that scales with a company’s success come to justify unsavory business practices or reckless accelerationism? And is this go-around any different from previous iterations of Silicon Valley giving?

“You can’t necessarily appeal to capitalism to solve some of the problems created by capitalist practices themselves … the exacerbation of extreme wealth concentration and massive inequalities,” says Linsey McGoey, professor of sociology at the University of Essex and author of No Such Thing as a Free Gift. “It’s like calling upon the arsonist to hose down the house he’s just set on fire.”

Silver formalized his charitable commitment through Founders Pledge, a nonprofit that helps entrepreneurs to give away their wealth. Unlike the Giving Pledge, a public but nonbinding commitment, Founders Pledge requires participants to enter into a contract. “The choice of making a binding pledge was very important,” says Silver.

Founders Pledge has been around since 2015. But the value of pledges recorded by the nonprofit has soared recently, from $400 million in 2023 to $4 billion so far this year. The AI industry now accounts for a third of the lifetime pledge total.

The organization’s goal, according to cofounder David Goldberg, is to identify “the very best ways to deploy capital at scale to make the world better.” It has frequently been lumped together with effective altruism, which encourages people to amass wealth in order to give it away, to rely on statistics rather than emotion, and to prioritize causes likely to have the biggest impact in the distant future. But despite the commonalities, Goldberg isn’t a fan of the comparison; Founders Pledge is concerned with human suffering in the present. “We’re far more humanist,” he says.

Silver considers himself an effective altruist but says his “flavor is about the here and now.” Accordingly, Silver plans to funnel his pledge proceeds to charities, like the Malaria Foundation, equipped to save the greatest number of lives in the near term. “I find it hard to justify focusing on the galactic future of humanity when there are millions of people suffering and dying today,” he says.

Osika, the Lovable founder, who has pledged to give away half of his equity proceeds, doesn’t identify as an effective altruist, but he shares the belief that amassing wealth by succeeding in business is the best way for him to maximize his personal impact on the world. “I think it’s a very good thing for people who are very thoughtful about the future of humanity to build [AI],” he tells WIRED.

The Gates Foundation—the most famous embodiment of techno-philanthropy—has given away more than $100 billion to causes targeting poverty and disease in the 25 years since it was founded by Bill and Melinda Gates. Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged to donate their $200 billion fortune to scientific research through their own foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. Both have been held up as shining examples of how an entrepreneurial mindset can translate into effective philanthropy and how the profit motive can be harnessed for good.

The new generation of AI philanthropists appear to want to carry that legacy forward, into a world they imagine will be utterly reorganized by superintelligence. “For a very long time, it’s been clear to me that this technological transformation is going to be the biggest thing that happens in our lives,” says Osika.

However, this type of giving can come with trade-offs, and can be used by megadonors to discreetly advance their political interests, McGoey says. A recent study found that a reliance on philanthropic funding led the WHO to prioritize donors’ preferred causes at the expense of other urgent issues, like non-communicable diseases.

Donations that alleviate issues stemming from wealth inequality instead of attacking the root cause, McGoey argues, threaten to end the debate about long-term, systemic remedies before it begins. “It’s appealing to the perpetuator of a problem to resolve it—and that doesn’t necessarily lead to positive results,” she says. “I don’t think that people should kid themselves that making money on its own is somehow noble.”

The WHO itself has acknowledged issues with its financing, and in 2022 it put forth a new model designed to address some of those concerns. Mark Suzman, the Gates Foundation’s CEO, has also recognized the pitfalls of relying on megadonors. “It’s not right for a private philanthropy to be one of the largest funders of multinational global health efforts,” he said in 2023, noting that the foundation had become the WHO’s second-largest donor. But he also put the blame on dwindling governmental contributions. “I’d love it if many more governments would pass us on that list,” he said.

Megadonors can play a valuable role in funding causes neglected for ideological reasons by governments, like family planning. But they’re not equally accountable, says Apolline Taillandier, a researcher at the University of Cambridge who specializes in political theory. “These funders are not elected. They have no need to account for their decisions,” she says. “It comes down to the question of whether philanthropy is the most legitimate way of redistributing resources.”

There is a further risk that entrepreneurs might treat their philanthropic ambition as moral justification for destructive behavior. In 2024, the one-time crypto kingpin and effective altruism poster boy Sam Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison for fraud. At trial, a former colleague testified that Bankman-Fried had based all of his decisions on cold statistical analysis, gladly risking disaster if it meant a chance at a sufficiently positive end result. The leaders of effective altruism declared Bankman-Friend an apostate, but others painted his fraud as a symptom of the movement's flawed moral logic.

In the context of artificial intelligence, the concern is that a charitable pledge could form part of a risk calculation. By Bankman-Friedian logic, the headlong pursuit of superintelligence would be justified, potential consequences be damned, if the money it creates will have a large enough philanthropic impact.

Silver denies that his pledge is part of some sort of moral accounting or a hedge against the possible negative outcomes of the AI race. He believes that superintelligence will have a radically positive impact, endlessly discovering new knowledge through a recursive cycle of trial and error.

Far from justifying reckless accelerationism, Silver argues, a pledge helps to eliminate the type of financial incentive that threatens to lead AI development astray. “Building a superintelligence company is a huge responsibility to the planet, and that responsibility shouldn’t be led by personal greed,” says Silver. “This was an intentional choice to make sure that whatever actions I take as an individual are for the benefit of humanity, not because there’s some enormous dollar figure that starts to appear on the horizon.”

Silver may be a beneficiary of an economic system stacked in his favor. But one of few ways he can redress that imbalance, he argues, is to give his money away. “Individuals that choose to use their money for good will have a massive, transformative difference on the future of the world we live in,” he says. “That’s independent of whether the macroeconomic situation is the right thing for humanity. It’s just a fact.”

entries.title: Census Proposal Would Stop Counting Undocumented Immigrants—and Ignore Race and Sexual Orientation
entries.summary: A draft rule reviewed by WIRED would prevent the census from counting undocumented immigrants. To protect against “distortions,” it would also bar questions about race and sexual orientation.
entries.content:
The US Department of Commerce, which oversees the Census Bureau, is circulating a proposed rule that would cease the collection of demographic data on racial minorities and LGBTQ+ people and prevent undocumented immigrants from being counted in the 2030 census, according to documents viewed by WIRED.

The decision could have far-reaching implications for federal funding, particularly in states where there are substantial numbers of racial and ethnic minorities, as well as on immigrant communities across the country.

The proposed rule, which is being circulated across government agencies for review, says the census will eliminate questions about race and sexual orientation “to protect from any distortions created from the inclusion of personal questions.” The memo also states that “illegal aliens (among others) should not be included in the apportionment count, they are not true inhabitants, members of the body politics [sic], or persons with ‘usual residence’ in the United States.”

This would likely require the reintroduction of a census question about a respondent’s citizenship. During Donald Trump’s first presidential term, Republicans attempted to add a citizenship question to the census for the first time since 1950. The effort was struck down by the Supreme Court, 5-4, with Chief Justice John Roberts siding with the Court’s then-larger liberal bloc on the grounds that the justification for adding the question was “contrived.” The decision did not, though, find that citizenship questions are inherently unconstitutional.

The Department of Commerce did not reply to requests for comment.

“This is about the Voting Rights Act,” says Danah Boyd, a professor at Cornell University who studies the census, referencing the landmark voter protection legislation that the Supreme Court dismantled earlier this year. Eliminating the collection of these data, she says, would make it difficult to make basic assessments, like whether a congressional district is predominantly made of minorities.

“If we don't know certain things, we can't challenge them politically,” says Boyd. “If we don't know that certain peoples live in a particular geography, we can't say, ‘Oh my gosh, here's some massive inequality.’”

Republicans and the Trump administration have long taken aim at the census. More recently, members of the Trump administration have attacked a little-known statistical method called “differential privacy,” which is used to prevent census data from being used to reidentify individual respondents, claiming that it makes the results inaccurate. In August 2025, Republican representative August Pfluger made another attempt to reintroduce a citizenship question on the census, sponsoring a bill called the COUNT Act, and in October, Republican senator Jim Banks of Indiana published a letter to Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, writing, “There is a credible argument that the framers of the Constitution designed the Census to cover lawful inhabitants and not those who are present illegally.”

Census questions are set between two and three years in advance of the actual survey, based on priorities set by the administration. The data from the census inform everything from the apportionment of congressional seats to federal funding that is allocated based on the size of a population.

An employee at the Department of Health and Human Services, who asked to remain anonymous because they are not authorized to speak to the press, tells WIRED that “many HHS programs use Census data to appropriate funding. Removing undocumented individuals from the census will cause localities with high numbers of those populations to lose critical federal funding.”

The employee says that removal of racial categories could specifically impact Native populations, which sometimes receive specialized funding. “Some programs use the ‘American Indian or Alaska Native’ category from the Census to make determinations of grants set aside for Tribal entities,” they say.

An employee at the Department of Commerce, who also spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the press, says that they are concerned that adding a citizenship question to the census would make people who are undocumented—or who have undocumented family members—afraid to be counted.

“Even if [the administration doesn't] do anything operationally like ICE or anything like that, they can make people feel as if they answer the Census they will be rounded up,” they say.

“When you eliminate people and when you make people too afraid to participate because of the eliminations of other peoples, you will actually purposefully suppress the number of people who are in a geography. And that is a way of trying to make certain that you erase their political power and their access to federal funding,” says Boyd.

entries.title: The Sharpest Image Ever Taken of the Sun Reveals a Hidden Phenomenon
entries.summary: The photograph, taken in visible light, made it possible to observe for the first time the tiny plasma vortices that had been predicted for more than a century.
entries.content:
For decades, scientists had theorized that the sun’s surface must be crisscrossed by tiny plasma vortices, generated by the interaction between its intense magnetic fields and the constantly flowing superheated material. This week, the world’s most powerful solar telescope has just confirmed this.

The latest image captured by the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope, located at the summit of Haleakalā volcano in Hawaii, shows for the first time evidence of the so-called Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, a physical phenomenon first predicted more than a century ago.

The image, shared by NASA, is not the most spectacular view of the sun, but it is one of the closest to how the human eye would see it if it could withstand the intense brightness. Unlike the famous photographs in shades of blue, green, or orange captured by space observatories using ultraviolet or X-ray radiation—wavelengths invisible to us—this image was captured in visible light. As a result, it reveals a landscape reminiscent of petals, swirls, and folds on the star’s surface.

What Exactly Does This Show?

The “petals” appearing in the image are generated by the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability. This occurs when two fluid currents move at different speeds. The friction between the two causes the boundary to ripple and form swirling patterns. The Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is not unique to the sun. It also occurs on Earth, for example, when wind blows over water or in clouds.

In the sun, the fluids are plasma streams—a state of matter in which gas is so hot that its atoms lose electrons. Scientists expected that, in certain regions of the sun, these plasma streams would behave just like two streams of air or water colliding with each other, forming vortices.

Until now, visible-light telescopes provided a seemingly smooth view of the sun. Thanks to the techniques used by the Inouye telescope, scientists were able to observe what is happening on its surface in much greater detail. Small vortices, barely a few dozen kilometers in diameter, are constantly forming and disappearing. These structures have always been there. We have only recently learned how to visualize them.

According to NASA, this image spans approximately the Earth’s radius and is the highest-resolution image available in visible light. The unprecedented details will provide a better understanding of how the sun transfers its energy to outer regions and how it alters the temperature of its solar corona. The solar corona is of great scientific interest, as it is the source of coronal mass ejections—the phenomena responsible for geomagnetic storms that threaten the world’s electronic systems.

This story originally appeared in WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
